name: Sunscreen-maxxing

lead: Sunscreen-maxxing means wearing sunscreen every day and reapplying it, to keep UV from building up photodamage: fewer wrinkles and dark spots, and smoother skin over the years.

Sunscreens filter or block UV radiation. SPF, introduced by Franz Greiter in 1974, mainly reflects UVB protection, and broad-spectrum labels indicate UVA protection too. A randomised Australian trial found that daily broad-spectrum use for 4.5 years was associated with smoother, more resilient skin than usual habits. Reference sources also report that sunscreen can help prevent melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma.

paras: People apply a broad-spectrum sunscreen on the face and exposed skin every morning and reapply through the day when outdoors. It is usually paired with other sun-protection habits and skincare. Studies find many people apply too little.
Reported issues include allergic contact dermatitis and, in some aerosols, benzene contamination. Typical use is not usually linked to vitamin D deficiency. Ingredient rules differ by country.

angle.text: Sunscreen-maxxing means strict daily SPF use with regular reapplication to limit UV-driven skin aging. Blocking UV means less photodamage accumulates, so fewer wrinkles and dark spots develop. A randomised Australian trial found smoother skin after 4.5 years of daily broad-spectrum use.

lead: Sunscreen-maxxing is the looksmaxxing term for strict daily use of sunscreen, with regular reapplication, to limit ultraviolet exposure and the skin ageing attributed to it.

Sunscreens are rated by sun protection factor (SPF), introduced by Franz Greiter in 1974, which mainly reflects protection against UVB.[1] Broad-spectrum products also protect against UVA.[1] Reference sources report that sunscreen can help prevent melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma, and a randomised trial in Australia found that daily broad-spectrum use for 4.5 years was associated with smoother, more resilient skin than usual habits.[1]
infobox: Sunscreen (OTC drug in the US; cosmetic in the EU)

paras: Practitioners apply sunscreen every day, including on cloudy days or indoors, and reapply during the day. Wikipedia reports that product directions usually advise reapplication about every two hours and after swimming.[1]

SPF expresses the fraction of burn-causing UV that reaches the skin under standardised application of 2 mg per square centimetre; for example SPF 15 allows roughly one-fifteenth through.[1] A higher SPF does not last longer on the skin, so reapplication is still advised.[1] Studies have found that many people apply a quarter to a half of the tested amount, which reduces the effective protection.[1]
Broad-spectrum labels denote UVA protection proportional to UVB protection under 2012 US FDA rules; the EU requires a UVA protection factor of at least one-third of the SPF.[1]

A 2013 trial in Australia, summarised on Wikipedia, followed about 900 participants; those assigned to daily broad-spectrum sunscreen for 4.5 years showed smoother, more resilient skin than those continuing usual use.[1] A smaller 32-person study reported that daily SPF 30 use reversed photoageing signs within 12 weeks, with the improvement lasting through a year.[1]

Reported adverse effects include allergic contact dermatitis, with oxybenzone and cinnamates listed as sensitisers.[1] Vitamin D deficiency is a stated concern, but the article says typical use does not usually cause it.[1] Independent testing found benzene contamination in 27 percent of aerosol sunscreens tested, leading to voluntary recalls.[1] The US banned PABA and trolamine salicylate as ingredients in 2021.[1]
Hawaii banned oxybenzone and octinoxate in 2018 and Palau banned several filters in 2020, citing coral reefs.[1]

timeline.event: H. A. Milton Blake formulates what is described as the first sunscreen (10% tannic acid).[1]
US FDA rules define broad spectrum labelling.[1]
